'''Florence Laura Goodenough''' (August 6, 1886 &ndash; April 4, 1959) was an American [[psychologist]] and [[professor]] at the [[University of Minnesota]] who studied child intelligence and various problems in the field of [[child development]]. She was president of the [[Society for Research in Child Development]] from 1946 to 1947. She is best known for publishing the book ''Measurement Of Intelligence By Drawings,'' where she introduced the ''Goodenough Draw-A-Man test (now the [[Draw-A-Person Test]])'' to assess intelligence in young children through nonverbal measurement.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Goodenough |first=Florence L. |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.268362?view=theater&ui=embed&wrapper=false |title=Measurement Of Intelligence By Drawings |year=1905 |via=[[The Internet Archive]]}}</ref> She is noted for developing the [[Minnesota Preschool Scale]]. In 1931, she published two books, titled ''Experimental Child Study''<ref>Benjamin, L. T. (1980). Women in Psychology: Biography and Autobiography. Psychology of Women Quarterly, 5(1), 140–144. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1471-6402.1981.tb01040.x</ref> (with [[John Edward Anderson (psychologist)|John E. Anderson]]) and ''Anger in Young Children,'' which analyzed the methods used in evaluating children.<ref name=":062">Thompson 1990</ref> She wrote the ''[[Handbook of Child Psychology]]'' in 1933, becoming the first known psychologist to critique ratio [[IQ]].

==Early life==
Florence Laura Goodenough was born on August 6, 1886 to Alice Gertrude Day and Linus North Goodenough in [[Honesdale, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Dong |first1=Catherine |last2=Peebles |first2=Mackenzie |last3=Pearson |first3=Laquitta |last4=Cota |first4=Andriana |date=2023-06-19 |title=Florence Goodenough |url=https://pressbooks.pub/openhistoryofpsychology/chapter/florence-goodenough/ |journal=Open History of Psychology: The Lives and Contributions of Marginalized Psychology Pioneers |language=en |via=pressbooks.pub}}</ref> She was the youngest child, with two brothers and six sisters. Her family was involved in farming.<ref name=":07">{{Cite book |last1=Ogilvie |first1=Marilyn Bailey |url=http://archive.org/details/biographicaldict00ogil_0 |title=The biographical dictionary of women in science: pioneering lives from ancient times to the mid-20th century |last2=Harvey |first2=Joy Dorothy |date=2000 |publisher=New York : Routledge |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-415-92038-4}}</ref> She was homeschooled and received the equivalent of a high school diploma.<ref name="Rodkey4">Rodkey, E. (2010). Profile of Florence L. Goodenough. In A. Rutherford (Ed.), Psychology's Feminist Voices Multimedia Internet Archive. Retrieved from http://www.feministvoices.com/florence_goodenough/{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Goodenough received her primary education at home until attending [[Millersville Normal School]]. This school had few options of careers for women, and she picked teaching. In 1908, Goodenough graduated from Millersville Normal School with a Bachelor of [[Pedagogy]]. There is not much documentation of her time at Millersville; however, it is known that after earning her degree, she moved on to teach at the University of Minnesota from 1912 to 1919.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Jolly |first=Jennifer |date=2010 |title=Florence L. Goodenough: Portrait of a Psychologist |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247528405 |access-date=April 24, 2023 |website=Research Gate}}</ref><ref name=":07"/> She then went back to college at [[Columbia University]]. She received a [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor of science]] in 1920, and a masters of art degree in 1921, under [[Leta Stetter Hollingworth|Leta Hollingworth]].<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":07"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Feminist Voices - Florence Goodenough |url=https://feministvoices.com/profiles/florence-goodenough |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=Feminist Voices |language=en}}</ref> Hollingworth was a psychologist and Goodenough's mentor. In 1921, Hollingworth recommended Goodenough to [[Lewis Terman]] to become a research assistant.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":07"/> From 1920 to 1921, she also served as the director of research for the Rutherford and [[Perth Amboy Public Schools|Perth Amboy]] public schools in the state of [[New Jersey]].<ref name=":222">{{Cite journal |last1=Johnston |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Johnson |first2=Ann |date=July 2017 |title=Balancing life and work by unbending gender: Early American women psychologists' struggles and contributions: JOHNSTON and JOHNSON |journal=Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences |language=en |volume=53 |issue=3 |pages=246–264 |doi=10.1002/jhbs.21862 |pmid=28722804}}</ref> It was during her time in public schools when she actually conducted a majority of her data.<ref name=":222"/> Goodenough then went to [[Stanford University]], beginning her doctoral studies by working with Lewis Terman on his Gifted Children Survey, which was later published as ''[[Genetic Studies of Genius]]''.<ref name=":12" /> 

Lewis originally assigned her to do field research for the paper in [[Los Angeles]]. She first served as the chief field psychologist, and then reached the higher status of chief research psychologist from 1922 to 1923, overseeing the other psychologists with her.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":07" /> She was listed as a contributor to Terman's book ''[[Genetic Studies of Genius]]''; at the time, it was rare for women to be listed as contributors to research.<ref name="Rogers22">Rogers, K. B. (1999). The Lifelong Productivity of the Female Research hers in Terman's Genetic Studies of Genius Longitudinal Study. Gifted Child Quarterly, 43: 150. DOI: 10.1177/001698629904300303</ref> Goodenough earned her PhD in psychology in 1924, from Stanford University.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":07" /> Goodenough then went to the University of Minnesota, a Child Welfare Institute, where she worked as a research professor under John E. Anderson from 1925 to 1930. Anderson and Goodenough were noted as offering some of the first undergraduate and graduate courses in [[developmental psychology]].<ref name=":34">{{Cite journal |last1=Benjamin |first1=Ludy T. |date=September 1980 |title=Women in Psychology: Biography and Autobiography |journal=Psychology of Women Quarterly |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=140–144 |doi=10.1111/j.1471-6402.1981.tb01040.x |issn=0361-6843 |s2cid=220992293}}</ref> She then became a professor of psychology from 1931 to 1947.<ref name=":07" />

== Major accomplishments ==
Goodenough studied psychology in a time where the study of [[nature vs. nurture]] was argued for what contributed more towards a child's development. Her mentor, Lewis Terman, believed nature was the more important factor for child development, arguing that the environment showed heavy influence in their personality and abilities in school. Two main areas of focus when discussing nature vs nurture effects were on a child's IQ and their emotional development. Goodenough opposed the previous well respected views, and believed it was the child's maturation that played the major role in a child's emotional development. She wanted to test the basis of fixed intelligence with the results shown through IQ testing. Defending these beliefs, she published books explaining her theories and thoughts on this in 1939–1940.<ref name=":07"/>

In addition to her time at the University of Minnesota, Goodenough created the [[draw-a-man test]], used to measure intelligence in children.<ref name="Jolly22">Jolly, J. L. (2010). Florence L. Goodenough: Portrait of a Psychologist. Roeper Review, 32:98–105. The Roeper Institute.</ref><ref name="Rodkey4" /><ref name="Harris22">Harris, D. (1959). Florence L. Goodenough, 1886–1959. Child Development, 30, 305–306.</ref><ref name="Plucker22">Plucker, J. A. (Ed.). (2003). Human intelligence: Historical influences, current controversies, teaching resources. Retrieved March 20, 2012.</ref> She published the test in ''Measurement of Intelligence'' (1926), including detailed accounts of procedures, scoring, and examples.<ref name=":07" /><ref name="Plucker22" /><ref name="Rodkey4" /> After her publication of the draw-a-man test, Goodenough expanded the [[Stanford-Binet Scale]] for children into the Minnesota Preschool Scale in 1932.<ref name=":07" /><ref name="Harris22" /><ref name="Plucker22" /> Goodenough's most significant contribution to psychology was her advancement of sampling in 1928, which would become to be known as [[Event sampling methodology|event]] and time sampling, a method that is still in use in the 21st century.<ref name=":07" /><ref name="Harris22" />

Goodenough published her time sampling approach in ''Anger in Young Children'' (1931), which analyzed the methods used in evaluating children. Her time sampling technique was critiqued for using mothers as research participants, with many doubting that nonscientists would successfully record observations for a study.<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal |last1=Louttit |first1=C. M. |date=1932 |title=[Review of The First Two Years; Anger in Young Children; Psychology of Infancy and Early Childhood; Mental Measurement of Pre-School Children and Negativism of Pre-School Children]. |url=http://content.apa.org/journals/apl/16/6/696 |journal=Journal of Applied Psychology |language=en |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=696–699 |doi=10.1037/h0067958 |issn=0021-9010|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":52">{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Ann |date=2015 |title=Florence Goodenough and child study: The question of mothers as researchers. |journal=History of Psychology |language=en |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=183–195 |doi=10.1037/a0038865 |issn=1939-0610 |pmid=26120919}}</ref> Goodenough's objective was to analyze [[John B. Watson]]'s<ref>{{cite web | url=https://feministvoices.com/profiles/florence-goodenough | title=Feminist Voices - Florence Goodenough }}</ref> assertion that newborns were primarily only capable of three different emotions: rage, fear, and love.<ref name=":42" /><ref name=":062">Thompson 1990</ref> She gathered forty-one participants, ranging from infancy through seven years old, and trained the parents to use event sampling and track the outbursts of anger they saw in their children.<ref name=":222"/><ref name=":062"/> It was through this experiment that she suggested that children who were less than one year old had the most notable triggers for anger, due to repetitive [[child care]], minimal physical irritations, and limitations of physical movement.<ref name=":52" /><ref name=":222" /><ref name=":062"/> However, Goodenough's research findings indicated that by the time the child reached the age of four, social interactions became the most significant basis of anger.<ref name=":222" /><ref name="Rodkey4"/><ref name=":062"/> Goodenough's findings led her to theorize that it was not the environment that was most influential in emotional development, but actually maturation in young children.<ref name=":34"/><ref name="Rogers22"/><ref name=":062"/> Overall, Goodenough's publication led to a crucial descriptive awareness for parents and professionals to help acknowledge diverse emotional inclinations in child development.<ref name=":34"/><ref name=":222" /><ref name=":062"/> This ultimately led her to continue with several more publications on child development, maturation, and emotion. Many researchers still appreciate Goodenough's publication on emotional development because of its detailed description of the [[methodology]] used.<ref name=":34"/><ref name=":42" /><ref name=":122">Florence L. Goodenough, 1886–1959. Child Development, 30, 305–306.</ref><ref name=":062"/> Goodenough's experiment represented one of the first large-scale analyses done through observations, and her research is still considered one of the most detailed analyses of emotional development in children.<ref name=":34"/><ref name=":42" /><ref name=":062"/>

== Women in war ==
Goodenough was an active [[feminist]] throughout her life, typified by her fight in [[Male-dominated occupation|male-dominated careers]] like psychology. She especially showed frustration when she and many other women were not allowed to participate in wartime jobs. The many psychology studies conducted involving the war were only being researched by men, while women were expected to volunteer in the local communities. Goodenough was the president of the [[National Council of Women Psychologists]] (NCWP), through which she fought for women psychologists to also be allowed to participate in wartime studies. She succeeded, and she and other women were able to obtain paid employment as military personnel.<ref name=":07"/>
[[File:RuthWinifredHoward1920.png|thumb|[[Ruth Winifred Howard]], one of the first African American women to earn a PhD in psychology. She was influenced and taught by Florence Goodenough. ]]

== Late life ==
Goodenough was never married.<ref name=":07"/> During her late career, Goodenough continued to publish on a variety of topics.<ref name=":34"/> She also was known as a great educator, and one of her students was [[Ruth Winifred Howard]], the first African American woman to receive a PhD in psychology.<ref name=":34" /><ref name=":062">Thompson 1990</ref> However, Goodenough was forced to retire early because she developed chronic diabetes and began to go blind and deaf.<ref name=":0" /> She moved to [[New Hampshire]],<ref name=":34" /> learned [[braille]], then published three more books: ''Mental Testing: Its History, Principles, and Applications'' (1949); ''Exceptional Children'' (1954); and the third edition of ''Developmental Psychology'' (1959).<ref name="Jolly22"/><ref name="Harris22"/> Altogether, Goodenough published 10 texts and 26 research articles.<ref name="faculty.frostburg.edu23">{{cite web |title=Psyography: Florence L. Goodenough |url=http://faculty.frostburg.edu/mbradley/psyography/florencegoodenough.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171017093542/http://faculty.frostburg.edu/mbradley/psyography/florencegoodenough.html |archive-date=2017-10-17 |website=faculty.frostburg.edu}}</ref> During this period, she spent summers in New Hampshire and [[Lisbon]], and her winters in [[Lakeland, Florida]].<ref name=":0" /> She died of a stroke in Lakeland on April 4, 1959.<ref name="Rodkey4"/><ref name="Harris22" /><ref name="Plucker22"/><ref name="faculty.frostburg.edu23" /><ref>Stevens, G. and Gardner, S. (1982). Florence Laura Goodenough. In G. Stevens and S. Gardner (Eds.), The women of psychology, Volume 1: Pioneers and innovators (pp. 193–197). Cambridge, MA.: Schenkman Publishing</ref>

==IQ testing==
Goodenough revised and invented tests for children. She studied exceptional children, child psychology, and anger and fear in children throughout her career.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/goodenough.htm|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170604104911/http://www.muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/goodenough.htm|archive-date=2017-06-04|title=Florence Goodenough|website=muskingum.edu|author=Compiled by Andria Bosler (May 2000)}}</ref> She published her first book: ''The Measurement of Intelligence by Drawings'' in 1926 which introduced her thoughts and ideas of children's IQ testing. In this book, Goodenough presented her [[IQ test]] for preschoolers called the [[Draw-a-man test|Draw-A-Man test.]] The test evaluates subjects based on the way they choose to draw a person. Goodenough was widely recognized for the test, which functions as a nonverbal measure of intelligence.<ref name="researchgate.net">{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247528405|title=Florence L. Goodenough: Portrait of a Psychologist|last1=Jolly|first1=Jennifer}}</ref> This test was initially geared towards children ages two through 13. The Draw-A-Man test eventually developed into a Draw-A-Woman Test due to critics believing many females would not necessarily be able to identify with a male.<ref>Goodenough, F. L. (1926). A new approach to the measurement of intelligence of young children. Ped. Sem, 33185–211.</ref>

The Draw-A-Man test measures children's' cognitive development levels. There has been no validation of the procedure as a personality test, or indeed as a test of anything other than cognitive development levels. In particular, research shows that the Draw-A-Man test does not measure IQ.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Imuta |first1=Kana |last2=Scarf |first2=Damian |last3=Pharo |first3=Henry |last4=Hayne |first4=Harlene |date=2013-03-14 |title=Drawing a Close to the Use of Human Figure Drawings as a Projective Measure of Intelligence |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=8 |issue=3 |article-number=e58991 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0058991 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=3597590 |pmid=23516590 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...858991I }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aikman |first1=Kerry G. |last2=Belter |first2=Ronald W. |last3=Finch Jr. |first3=A. J. |date=1992 |title=Human figure drawings: Validity in assessing intellectual level and academic achievement |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/1097-4679%28199201%2948%3A1%3C114%3A%3AAID-JCLP2270480116%3E3.0.CO%3B2-Y |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=114–120 |doi=10.1002/1097-4679(199201)48:1<114::AID-JCLP2270480116>3.0.CO;2-Y |issn=1097-4679|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Academic work and contributions ==
{{prose|date=August 2024}}
Director of research for the Rutherford & Perth Amboy public schools (1920–1921)

Research assistant in Psychology under Lewis Terman, Stanford University (1921–1925).

Assistant Professor under John E. Anderson (1925–1930)

Published her first book- ''The Measurement of Intelligence by Drawings'' (1926)

Published the ''Draw-a-Man test'' (1926)

Published ''Anger in Young Children'' and the ''Measurement of Mental Growth'' (1931)

Published ''Minnesota Preschool Scale'' (1932)

Full time professor at the University of Minnesota (1931–1947)

President of the National Counsel of Women Psychologists (1942)

President of the Society for Research in Child Development (1946–1947).

==Timeline==
{{prose timeline|date=August 2024}}
* 1886: Born in Honesdale, Pennsylvania
* 1908: Bachelor of Pedogogy (B.Pd.) earned from Normal School in Millersville, Pennsylvania.
* 1920: B.S. from Columbia University under [[Leta Hollingworth]].
* Director of Research in the Rutherford and Perth Amboy New Jersey public schools.
* Began to document the effects of environment on intelligence test scores.
* 1921: M.A. earned from Columbia University under Leta Hollingsworth.
* First began working with Lewis Terman at Stanford University.
* 1923: Published The Stanford Achievement Test.
* 1924: PhD Philosophy earned from Stanford University under Lewis Terman.
* Worked at Minneapolis Child Guidance Clinic.
* 1925: Appointed assistant professor in the Institute of Child Welfare at the University of Minnesota.
* 1926: Published her first book: ''The Measurement of Intelligence by Drawings'' (Introduction to Draw-A-Man test).
* 1931: Published ''The Measurement of Mental Growth''.
* Published ''Anger in Young Children''.
* Goodenough set out to evaluate J. B. Watson's claim that newborns were initially only capable of three emotions: rage, fear and love, by comparing children's anger in infancy and in childhood. The book reported findings that children show anger at bath time, physical discomfort, and by age four, social relations were the greatest source of anger.<ref name=webster />{{Unreliable source?|date=September 2021|sure=y|reason=This is an unpublished undergraduate student assignment paper}}
* Promoted to full professor in the Institute of Child Welfare at the University of Minnesota.
* 1933: Published ''Handbook of Child Psychology.''
* 1938: Served as president of the National Council of Women Psychologists.
* 1940: Goodenough–Harris drawing test established, as revised by Florence Goodenough and Dale Harris.
* 1947: Retired early from the University of Minnesota due to physical illness.
* 1942: The [[Women's Army Corps|Women's Army Auxiliary Corps]] (WAAC) solicited Goodenough's professional opinion in selection of tests to be given to Officer Candidates and Basics. Goodenough recommended the Goodenough Speed-of-Association Test. The test used free association to determine ratings of masculinity–femininity and leadership. Results from Candidates and Basics were used as norming data as the test was under construction. She was particularly interested in how results differed between women who were married, divorced, or single. She found that divorced women were more masculine and offered a greater percentage of rare responses compared to either of the two other groups. Early retirement cut short her work on this test and it was never completed.<ref name=webster>{{Cite web|url=http://faculty.webster.edu/woolflm/goodenough.html|title=Florence Goodenough 1886-1959|last1=Weiss|first1=Adrian}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=September 2021|sure=y|reason=This is an unpublished undergraduate student assignment paper}}
* 1947: Appointed [[Professor Emeritus]] until her death in 1959.
* 1949: Published ''Mental Testing: Its History, Principles, and Applications''.
* 1956: Published Exceptional Children.
* Died from a stroke at the age of 73.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/goodenough.htm#Time%20Line|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170604104911/http://www.muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/goodenough.htm#Time%20Line|archive-date=2017-06-04|website=muskingum.edu|title=Florence Goodenough|author=Compiled by Andria Bosler (May 2000)}}</ref>
